column1: Substance use disorder involves impaired control|F|25423|A substance use disorder is a persistent pattern of use that causes clinically significant impairment or distress. Features can include impaired control, strong motivation to obtain the substance, and continued use despite harmful consequences. The diagnosis concerns behavior and functioning, not simply whether someone has ever used a drug.|Physical dependence means the body has adapted so that stopping or reducing exposure produces withdrawal. Tolerance means a given amount produces a smaller effect after repeated exposure. Either can occur during appropriate medical treatment and does not by itself establish compulsive use.|Researchers isolate reinforcement and learning using tasks with defined consequences. The mouse shown here explores an apparatus before reward-related stimulation is introduced. This baseline measures where it normally moves, allowing later preference to be distinguished from a pre-existing attraction to one location.

Reinforcement changes the probability of an action|F|25423|Positive reinforcement strengthens an action because it produces a desirable consequence. Negative reinforcement strengthens an action because it removes an unpleasant condition. Both processes increase future responding, even though one adds an outcome and the other removes one.|Punishment instead reduces an action through its consequences. The word negative in negative reinforcement therefore does not mean punishment or harm. For example, relief of withdrawal can strengthen drug taking because the action temporarily removes an aversive bodily state.|Reinforcement is defined by the observed change in behavior rather than the researcher's intention. An offered reward may fail to strengthen responding, while an apparently unpleasant event can have different effects in different circumstances. The action and its contingent consequence must be measured together.

An operant action earns a defined reward|R|86183|OHRBETS is an experimental system for studying reward and aversion in head-fixed mice. The animal can turn a small lever while receiving controlled outcomes. Head fixation stabilizes recordings, while the lever preserves an action whose consequence can be changed by the experimenter.|The original recording follows lever turns that earn sucrose under fixed-ratio schedules. A fixed ratio specifies how many responses are required for an outcome. Changing that requirement alters the action cost while leaving the basic reward and response available to the animal.|The study combined such tasks with measurements of dopamine-related activity and consumption. This makes the action, outcome delivery, and neural signal separately observable. The selected demonstration concerns food reinforcement, providing a defined learning process rather than a recording of compulsive drug taking.

The speed of drug delivery changes reinforcement|F|25423|A psychoactive drug changes nervous-system function after reaching relevant targets. Its effects depend on absorption, distribution, metabolism, and removal, as well as receptor action. The same molecule can therefore have different time courses when it enters the body by different routes.|Rapid delivery can produce a steep rise in brain concentration and make an action's consequence closely follow that action. Close timing helps reinforcement and cue learning. Longer-lasting exposure produces a different pattern of receptor occupancy even when the total amount reaching the body is comparable.|Delivery kinetics do not determine all risk independently of the person or setting. Prior learning, availability, stress, and biological sensitivity also shape continued use. The mechanistic distinction is between how quickly a drug reaches its target and what it does after arriving there.

A learned place preference persists without stimulation|R|25423|Researchers stimulated dopamine-containing axons from the ventral tegmental area to the medial olfactory tubercle in mice. During training, stimulation occurred in a designated part of the apparatus. The medial olfactory tubercle is a reward-related forebrain region that also receives odor information.|The selected post-training recording tests location preference without ongoing light delivery. Mice returned preferentially to the region previously associated with stimulation. The response therefore depended on the learned value of the location rather than light forcing movement at that instant.|The study compared this test with pre-training exploration in the same apparatus. Measuring both stages separated acquired preference from ordinary spatial bias. The specific projection terminates in medial olfactory tubercle, so this experiment should not be described as stimulation of nucleus accumbens terminals.

Mesolimbic dopamine helps reinforce learned actions|F|25423|The ventral tegmental area, or VTA, contains dopamine neurons that project to forebrain regions including the nucleus accumbens. The accumbens is part of the ventral striatum and helps translate motivational information into action. Dopamine changes how these circuits respond to inputs and learn from outcomes.|Many reinforcing drugs increase dopamine signaling through different initial targets. Some act on transporters, while others alter neurons that control dopamine-cell firing. A shared downstream change therefore does not mean that every drug binds the same receptor or produces the same physiological effects.|Dopamine is not a direct meter of pleasure. Its activity varies with predictions, salience, movement, and other task conditions. To interpret a dopamine signal, researchers must identify its location, the event that changed it, and the behavior being measured at that time.

Stimulation can establish a location's value|R|25423|In the first training recording, entering the designated apparatus region triggers stimulation of VTA axons in medial olfactory tubercle. The consequence is spatially contingent: the animal's position controls when the light is delivered. This permits the location to acquire value through repeated experience.|The investigators later tested the location without stimulation and found a learned preference. Training and testing therefore address different stages. The training recording shows the contingency being experienced, while the later test measures whether the animal retains an attraction to the previously paired region.|Stimulating an identified dopamine projection bypasses the initial pharmacological targets through which drugs normally act. It tests the contribution of that pathway to reinforcement-related learning. The preparation establishes a causal role for the projection without requiring administration of a reinforcing drug in this demonstration.

Striatal dopamine receptors regulate different cells|F|85064|D1-like and D2-like receptors are major families through which dopamine changes cellular signaling. They influence enzymes that regulate cyclic AMP, an intracellular messenger. Their effects depend on the cell and its other inputs rather than directly encoding one universal good or bad outcome.|The ventral striatum contributes to motivation and reinforcement, while dorsal-striatal systems participate in action selection and well-practiced behavior. Repeated drug experience can alter activity and plasticity across these systems. Compulsive responding is therefore not explained by one brief dopamine increase alone.|The prefrontal cortex contributes to evaluating consequences and controlling actions according to goals. Its development and current physiological state influence these functions. Drug-related behavior reflects interactions among motivational signals, learned actions, and control systems rather than a complete loss of all deliberate choice.

A looming stimulus can change accumbens dopamine|R|85064|A mouse study measured dopamine signals in the lateral nucleus accumbens during visual events. The researchers used dLight, a fluorescent sensor whose brightness changes when dopamine binds. This measured local dopamine-related fluorescence while the mouse encountered different patterns of illumination.|The original looming-stimulus recording shows the animal's movement during an expanding visual event. Such a stimulus can resemble an approaching overhead object and evoke defense. The investigators compared its sensory features with other visual presentations rather than treating any dopamine response as evidence of pleasure.|The dopamine signal tracked the rate and magnitude of illumination change more closely than the inferred threat level. A response to the visual event therefore required a sensory explanation. This finding separates a measured transmitter signal from the emotional label assigned to the event by an observer.

Adolescence and environment influence vulnerability|F|85064|Adolescence includes continuing development of circuits involved in motivation, learning, and behavioral control. Experiences during this period can alter later responses to rewards and cues. Increased vulnerability does not mean that every adolescent exposure inevitably produces a substance use disorder.|Genetic variation can influence drug metabolism, receptor function, or sensitivity to effects. Environmental conditions influence availability, stress, social learning, and alternative rewards. Risk develops through their interaction rather than one gene determining a fixed outcome independently of experience.|Repeated exposure also changes the nervous system through learning and cellular adaptation. These acquired changes must be separated from differences present before use began. A study that measures people only after a disorder develops cannot by itself establish which biological differences preceded the repeated exposure.

Visual timing changes the measured dopamine response|R|85064|The accumbens study systematically varied the visual stimulus rather than presenting only one threatening image. The selected original stimulus movie shows the patterns used in the experiments. It is the publisher's task presentation, separate from the accompanying recordings of freely moving animals.|Changing how quickly illumination rose or fell changed the dopamine-related response. Wavelength also affected the response, consistent with sensory processing contributing to the signal. These comparisons tested properties of the input that would remain hidden if all stimuli were classified only as threatening or neutral.|The researchers also examined pathway-related controls to establish that the fluorescent response was not simply an arbitrary movement trace. The central finding remained stimulus-specific: local dopamine tracked defined changes in illumination. This is a measured sensory response, not proof that dopamine has no role in reinforcement elsewhere.

A transmitter response need not report hedonic value|R|85064|Hedonic value concerns how pleasant or unpleasant an experience is. Incentive value concerns how strongly it attracts behavior, and a sensory response concerns detection of an event's features. These quantities can vary together in some tasks without being interchangeable measurements.|The lateral-accumbens experiment dissociated visual features from the assumed threatening significance of the stimulus. Its dopamine signal changed with illumination dynamics even when a pleasure interpretation would be implausible. The anatomical location and experimental event specified what was measured.|This does not require abandoning dopamine's established roles in reinforcement. Different projections and local circuits can carry different mixtures of information. A drug-induced dopamine increase must therefore be interpreted within the relevant circuit and learned behavior, rather than equating fluorescence amplitude with enjoyment.

A spotlight provides a different visual challenge|R|85064|The selected spotlight recording follows a mouse during a localized illumination change. It provides a real behavioral comparison with the looming stimulus. The two visual events differ in their spatial and temporal structure, allowing sensory properties to be assessed alongside the animal's movement.|The study found that dopamine in lateral accumbens followed illumination dynamics across these comparisons. The response could not be explained simply by assigning a larger threat value to every stimulus with a larger signal. The measured relationship concerned how the incoming light changed.|The animal's locomotion and the transmitter measurement answer different questions. One describes the action that occurred during the visual event; the other follows a chemical signal in a defined region. Keeping these measurements separate prevents movement or arousal from being silently renamed as pleasure.

One apparatus separates distinct reward measures|R|86183|The OHRBETS researchers designed tasks that separated action, delivery, and consumption. A mouse could perform the lever response before receiving the outcome, and licking provided another measure after delivery. These events do not necessarily occur at the same moment or reflect the same motivational process.|The system also allowed outcomes to vary in value or aversiveness while recording behavior under stable imaging conditions. Comparing these phases helped identify whether a neural signal accompanied seeking, receiving, or consuming. A response during consumption cannot automatically be assigned to anticipation of the outcome.|Head fixation changes the available movements, but the animal still controls a defined action-outcome contingency. The experimental claim concerns that contingency and the recorded signals. It does not require treating every lever turn as equivalent to unrestricted seeking of a drug in a natural environment.

An action can gain stimulation or terminate it|R|86183|The original paired OHRBETS demonstration contains two reinforcement arrangements. In one, responding obtains optical stimulation of lateral-hypothalamic GABA neurons. In the other, responding turns off stimulation of a lateral-hypothalamic glutamate population. The consequence of the action differs between the two panels.|The first arrangement tests positive reinforcement through obtaining an outcome. The second tests negative reinforcement through removal of an ongoing aversive condition. Responding to terminate stimulation is therefore different from receiving stimulation as a punishment for the response.|The same basic action can be strengthened by either consequence. This makes the direction of the contingency essential for interpreting the behavior. The demonstration provides a direct experimental distinction relevant to drug seeking for reward versus drug seeking to relieve an unpleasant state.

Withdrawal can supply negative reinforcement|F|86183|With repeated exposure, nervous-system adaptations can oppose a drug's acute effects. When drug concentrations fall, those adaptations can contribute to withdrawal. The symptoms depend on the drug and can include bodily discomfort, altered mood, sleep disturbance, and strong motivation to restore the previous state.|Taking the drug again may temporarily reduce these symptoms. Relief then negatively reinforces the action, adding a maintaining process beyond the initial rewarding effect. The person can continue responding even when the pleasurable effect has diminished or use has become harmful.|Withdrawal and craving are related but distinct. Craving can also be triggered by cues, stress, or memories after acute withdrawal has subsided. A treatment that controls withdrawal therefore addresses an important maintaining process without necessarily eliminating every learned trigger for future use.

Consumption varies with the available outcome|R|86183|The OHRBETS multi-spout task presented solutions differing in salt concentration. The selected original recording follows licking across the available conditions. Consumption could therefore be measured directly rather than inferred solely from the work the animal performed to obtain access.|The investigators used these kinds of comparisons to examine how outcome properties influence behavior and neural signals. A change in licking reflects the animal's interaction with the delivered solution. It is a consummatory measure, distinct from lever responding before the outcome arrives.|The example concerns salt solutions rather than drug self-administration. Its relevance is the separation of seeking from consuming under controlled conditions. Changes in a dopamine-related signal can be aligned with these different events instead of assuming one value represents every phase of reinforcement.

A specific dopamine projection supports odor learning|R|25423|The VTA-to-olfactory-tubercle study also paired odors with stimulation of the identified dopamine projection. An odor could therefore acquire value without being intrinsically preferred before training. The investigators tested the learned odor preference after the pairing procedure.|Blocking dopamine receptors in medial olfactory tubercle prevented the stimulation-related odor preference. This intervention acted at the terminal region rather than changing the smell itself. Dopamine signaling in that target was therefore necessary for the tested learning effect.|In a further manipulation, reducing activity in VTA neurons projecting to medial olfactory tubercle disrupted learned odor preference and odor-based discrimination learning. The projection thus contributed to both acquiring and expressing value-guided responses involving sensory information received by its forebrain target.

An odor can retrieve an acquired preference|R|25423|The selected original recording follows an odor-preference test after odor and dopamine-projection stimulation had been paired. The light-based training event is no longer required at every choice. The odor itself can guide where the mouse investigates because of the earlier learning.|The experiment distinguishes the sensory cue from the reinforcing event associated with it. A cue does not need to contain a drug or directly activate a receptor to influence later behavior. Its acquired value depends on the history of pairings and the neural systems that store and retrieve that history.|The study's pathway manipulations identified medial olfactory tubercle dopamine signaling as a contributor to this learning. The animal's later preference is therefore more than a response to immediate stimulation. It is an observable choice controlled by a previously neutral sensory cue.

Cues and stress can renew drug seeking|F|25423|Drug-associated cues include places, objects, people, and internal sensations repeatedly paired with use. Through learning, they can attract attention and evoke expectations before the drug is present. Their influence can persist beyond the period of acute intoxication or withdrawal.|In reinstatement experiments, an animal first learns to obtain a drug and later experiences sessions without it. A cue, stressor, or drug-related event can then increase previously reduced responding. The renewed action is measured separately from whether the animal actually receives the drug during the test.|Stress can also increase the motivation to seek relief and alter regulation of learned responses. Recovery therefore includes managing cues and stress as well as drug clearance. The persistence of learned triggers helps explain why simply waiting for a substance to leave the body does not remove every source of risk.

Opioids act on receptors in several circuits|F|49319|Opioid receptors normally respond to peptide messengers produced by the body. Mu, delta, and kappa receptors belong to a family that communicates through G proteins inside cells. Opioid drugs differ in how strongly and selectively they activate these receptor types.|In some VTA circuits, mu-receptor activation inhibits GABA-releasing cells or terminals that restrain dopamine neurons. Reducing that inhibition can increase dopamine-cell activity. This is disinhibition: inhibiting an inhibitory input allows the receiving neuron to become more active.|Opioid receptors also occur in pain pathways, brainstem circuits, and peripheral tissues. Their actions can therefore include analgesia, sedation, constipation, and respiratory suppression. Reinforcement and pain relief are different consequences of receptor activation at different cellular locations.

Fluorescent labeling identifies mu receptors|R|49319|Researchers developed a probe that labels opioid receptors in living tissue without permanently occupying their drug-binding site. A receptor-binding guide brings a fluorescent tag near the receptor. After the tag is transferred, the guide can leave while the receptor remains visible.|The original depth sequence follows labeled mu receptors in the locus coeruleus of an FMOR mouse, which expresses a tagged receptor. Moving through successive optical planes reveals receptor-bearing structures within the tissue. It is a receptor-localization recording, distinct from drug-induced reinforcement or withdrawal.|The investigators tested whether labeled receptors retained function after the reaction. A probe that blocks its target would change the biology being studied. The method allowed receptor location and later physiological responses to be examined in a living preparation.

Tolerance and dependence involve adaptation|F|81298|Tolerance is a reduction in a drug's effect after repeated exposure to a comparable amount. Adaptation can occur at receptors, intracellular pathways, or larger circuits. The degree of tolerance can differ among effects produced by the same drug, so one change cannot be assumed to protect against every adverse effect.|Physical dependence becomes evident when reduced exposure produces withdrawal. Cells that adapted during ongoing drug action now operate without the condition they had been counteracting. The resulting symptoms reflect altered regulation, not simply the presence of drug molecules remaining in the body.|Tolerance and dependence can coexist with a substance use disorder, but neither is its complete definition. Impaired control and continued use despite harmful consequences require separate assessment. Receptor experiments identify particular cellular adaptations rather than directly diagnosing those behavioral features.

Mu receptors leave the axonal surface after activation|R|81298|A study in cultured rat striatal neurons followed opioid receptors in axons. Fluorescent labels distinguished receptors from presynaptic structures and internal sorting compartments. Adding the mu-receptor agonist DAMGO caused receptors to move from the cell surface into the axon's interior.|This uptake is endocytosis, in which membrane and associated proteins enter internal vesicles. The original movie follows receptor redistribution alongside labeled cellular compartments. It records movement of receptor protein rather than a direct measurement of how strongly an intact animal experiences an opioid.|Over longer exposure, repeated internalization and recycling reduced the available axonal surface pool. Fewer surface receptors can reduce the response to later stimulation. The study therefore identified a trafficking mechanism that contributes to tolerance at presynaptic opioid receptors.

Opioid G-protein signaling reduces transmitter release|F|81298|When an opioid receptor activates an inhibitory G protein, its components influence several cellular targets. They can reduce cyclic AMP production and regulate ion channels. The resulting effect depends on whether the receptor is located on a cell body, dendrite, or presynaptic terminal.|At a presynaptic terminal, reducing calcium-channel activity can decrease transmitter release. Calcium entry normally helps trigger fusion of transmitter-filled vesicles with the membrane. Less entry can therefore weaken the chemical signal sent to the next cell.|On some neurons, opioid signaling also increases potassium conductance and reduces excitability. These actions explain how receptor activation can suppress cellular output. The behavior produced by that suppression depends on what the affected cell normally does within its circuit.

Delta receptors follow a different trafficking pattern|R|81298|The same axonal study compared delta opioid receptors with mu receptors. Both could be internalized after activation, but their later handling differed. Comparing receptor types in a shared preparation helped identify whether the trafficking effect depended on the receptor rather than the general presence of an axon.|The selected delta-receptor movie follows redistribution after the delta agonist DADLE is added. Receptor fluorescence moves relative to presynaptic and internal-compartment labels. This is the delta-receptor preparation, not another view of the mu-receptor experiment.|Delta receptors recycled less effectively in the tested axons and showed stronger loss of the surface response over prolonged activation. Receptor return to the membrane therefore influenced later signaling. Removing a receptor from the surface and restoring it afterward are separate steps with different functional consequences.

Endosomes sort receptors after internalization|F|81298|An endosome is a membrane-bound compartment that receives material taken in from the cell surface. Internalized receptors can be sorted toward recycling routes or toward degradation. The destination determines whether the surface receptor pool can be restored after an agonist-induced uptake event.|Recycling returns receptors to the membrane, where they can again encounter extracellular drug or transmitter. Degradation instead breaks down the receptor and requires replacement by newly made protein. The balance between these routes can change responsiveness during repeated or prolonged exposure.|After internalization, some receptors can continue signaling from inside the cell. Sorting then determines whether their next destination is the surface or a degradative compartment. Recycling restores access to extracellular agonists, whereas degradation removes the receptor protein and makes recovery depend on replacement.

Phosphorylation changes separate receptor mechanisms|R|81298|Phosphorylation adds a phosphate group to a protein and can change how other proteins interact with it. The axonal study examined receptor-tail sites that receive these modifications. For mu receptors, GRK2/3 enzymes contributed to the phosphorylation-dependent internalization process.|The selected recording instead follows a delta receptor whose tail serine and threonine sites were replaced. This mutant still underwent agonist-induced internalization in the tested preparation. Delta-receptor uptake therefore did not require the same tail-phosphorylation arrangement as the mu-receptor mechanism.|The comparison separates receptor activation from the machinery that moves the receptor afterward. Two opioid receptor types can inhibit signaling acutely while relying on different rules for internalization and recycling. Those rules help explain why their longer-term axonal tolerance differs.

Receptor regulation depends on the agonist|F|81298|An agonist activates a receptor after binding, but different agonists can stabilize different receptor states. The resulting balance among G-protein signaling, phosphorylation, and internalization can vary. Equal receptor binding therefore does not guarantee equal trafficking over time.|A partial agonist produces less activation than a full agonist under comparable conditions in a defined system. Its effect also depends on receptor number and the cell's signaling capacity. Partial activation is not the same as failing to bind or having no physiological effect.|Biased signaling describes a preference among a receptor's downstream responses relative to a comparison condition. This must be measured in an actual preparation. A label such as biased does not by itself establish that a drug is free of tolerance, respiratory effects, or misuse potential in people.

Baseline imaging follows striatal neuronal calcium|R|Frontiers1347491|A rat study examined how astrocytes regulate neurons in dorsal striatum after cocaine self-administration. Astrocytes are non-neuronal cells that influence conditions around synapses. Researchers altered their calcium regulation and measured neuronal activity in slices obtained after the animals' training.|The selected original recording shows neuronal GCaMP fluorescence in artificial cerebrospinal fluid before acute cocaine is applied. GCaMP becomes brighter when intracellular calcium rises. The changing signal follows calcium events in neurons, rather than directly measuring dopamine release or the animal's motivation.|This baseline field provides the comparison for the same preparation after cocaine exposure. Its position in the experiment is important: the tissue is being recorded outside the animal. Drug seeking was measured separately in the behavioral portion of the study.

Cocaine and amphetamine alter dopamine differently|F|Frontiers1347491|Dopamine transporters normally remove released dopamine from extracellular space by returning it to presynaptic terminals. Cocaine blocks this transporter and prolongs dopamine availability after release. It also affects other monoamine transporters, contributing to effects beyond one dopamine pathway.|Amphetamine enters monoamine terminals and changes the handling of stored transmitter. Its actions can increase cytosolic dopamine and promote outward transport through the dopamine transporter. This differs from simply blocking reuptake while leaving all intracellular transmitter handling unchanged.|Both drugs can increase extracellular dopamine, but their cellular routes and time courses differ. Repeated exposure can also alter learning and circuit regulation. The shared increase in a transmitter does not erase distinctions in the initial pharmacology or later physiological consequences.

Acute cocaine changes neuronal calcium in the same field|R|Frontiers1347491|The paired original recording follows the neuronal field after cocaine is applied to the slice. Comparing it with the preceding baseline avoids attributing differences between unrelated fields to the acute drug. The movie reports calcium fluorescence, with the source's accelerated playback preserved.|In the study, acute cocaine reduced neuronal calcium-event amplitude across the tested groups. Prior self-administration changed other aspects of astrocyte control over neurons, but did not abolish this acute response. Acute drug action and experience-dependent regulation were therefore measured separately.|Reducing astrocyte calcium increased cue-induced reinstatement of cocaine seeking in the behavioral experiment. It also increased neuronal-event amplitude specifically after cocaine self-administration. These results identify a contribution of astrocyte regulation to later cue responding, beyond the immediate action of cocaine in the slice.

Drug cues can gain control over action selection|F|Frontiers1347491|Repeated pairing allows drug-related cues to predict the drug's effects. A cue can then capture attention, increase expectation, or initiate a well-practiced action sequence. Its influence is learned even though the cue itself does not reproduce the drug's full receptor-level effects.|Dorsal-striatal circuits contribute to organizing actions and routines. With repeated experience, behavior can become less dependent on actively evaluating the current outcome at every step. This does not imply that all drug seeking is automatic or that consequences have no influence.|Prefrontal and limbic inputs continue to interact with these action systems. Stress and physiological state can change which signals dominate a choice. Relapse risk therefore concerns both stored cue associations and the current conditions under which those associations are retrieved.

Mice can perform an intranasal self-administration task|R|s41467-025-65875-w|A recent study developed an operant task in which head-restrained male mice obtained intranasal cocaine. The animal's responses controlled delivery under a fixed-ratio schedule. This provided a route-specific preparation for examining voluntary drug taking while maintaining stable access for neural measurements.|The original movie follows responding in the apparatus, with cues marking delivery-related events. It is a task demonstration rather than instructions for human use. The research comparison concerned schedule-dependent responding and verified exposure after the animal earned the outcome.|Self-administration differs from an experimenter giving every animal the same noncontingent treatment. In the operant task, the animal's action changes whether an outcome occurs. This contingency permits reinforcement and drug-related cues to be studied together in a controlled preparation.

Sensitization and craving are different outcomes|F|s41386-026-02350-0|Sensitization means that a response becomes larger after repeated exposure. Psychomotor sensitization concerns changes in movement-related effects of a drug. Tolerance is a reduction in a response under comparable conditions, so the same exposure history can affect different outcomes in different directions.|Incentive salience concerns the ability of a cue or expected outcome to attract and energize behavior. It is related to wanting rather than necessarily to pleasure. A larger motor response after a drug does not directly establish stronger cue-triggered motivation before the drug arrives.|Experiments must therefore measure movement, cue-directed approach, and intake separately. Their correlations can change across individuals and stages of exposure. A behavioral marker predicts escalation only if its relationship with later intake is tested rather than assumed from the size of an acute drug response.

Pre-session cue responses predicted intake escalation|R|s41386-026-02350-0|Researchers followed cocaine self-administration in genetically heterogeneous rats and used pose-estimation software to track movement. They compared psychomotor sensitization or tolerance with behavior before drug access. This separated drug-induced movement from approach in anticipation of the session.|Pre-session locomotion and approaches to the active-lever area predicted later escalation more effectively than the measured sensitization or tolerance. The findings concerned incentive-related responding before intake. The selected SLEAP recording demonstrates tracking in representative sensitized and tolerant animals, not a direct readout of subjective craving.|Some initially lower-responding rats developed stronger anticipatory behavior and increased intake with extended experience. Vulnerability therefore changed across exposure rather than remaining fixed by the earliest response. The study's longitudinal measures distinguished a developing motivational pattern from one isolated motor effect.

Epac2 regulates cocaine reinforcement|R|80747|Cyclic AMP is a messenger inside cells that changes the activity of downstream proteins. Epac2 is one protein activated by cyclic AMP in neurons. Researchers tested whether Epac2 in midbrain dopamine cells contributes to cocaine reinforcement by altering dopamine release.|Removing Epac2 from dopamine neurons reduced evoked dopamine release in nucleus accumbens and reduced cocaine self-administration. A selective Epac2 inhibitor also reduced responding in the tested tasks. These interventions acted on cellular regulation rather than directly blocking cocaine's binding to the dopamine transporter.|Artificially increasing dopamine-neuron activity restored release and reversed the self-administration deficit in the conditional knockout. This rescue connected the behavioral effect to dopamine output. The experiment identifies a candidate cellular mechanism in mice rather than an established clinical Epac2 treatment for cocaine use disorder.

IL-13 can suppress VTA dopamine activity|R|s41380-025-03137-3|Interleukin-13, or IL-13, is a cytokine that can also be produced by cells in the nervous system. Researchers found its receptor component IL-13R alpha-1 on VTA dopamine neurons. They tested whether this signal changes the cells' activity and their response to nicotine.|Applying IL-13 reduced spontaneous dopamine-neuron activity. The selected calcium recording follows labeled VTA dopamine cells during the treatment. Its fluorescence reports changes in cellular calcium, while separate electrical recordings measured changes in firing.|The effect required the relevant receptor and intracellular signaling involving PI3K and AKT enzymes. Functional HCN channels were also required for the inhibitory response. These experiments identify a specific neuroimmune influence on dopamine cells, rather than treating every cytokine as a uniform source of excitation.

IL-13 opposes nicotine's stimulation of dopamine cells|R|s41380-025-03137-3|Nicotine increased activity in the tested VTA dopamine preparation, while IL-13 opposed that response. The original second recording follows the treatment comparison with nicotine and IL-13. It shows the cellular response under those conditions rather than the behavior of an animal seeking nicotine.|The study combined calcium imaging with electrical recordings and receptor-related manipulations. Removing the relevant IL-13 receptor component prevented the expected inhibitory action. This distinguished an identified receptor mechanism from a nonspecific reduction in activity caused by adding any protein to the preparation.|Delivering IL-13 locally to VTA also reduced nicotine self-administration in the rodent experiments. The behavioral result followed a targeted brain manipulation, not a clinical trial of systemic cytokine treatment. The cellular and behavioral findings describe different measured stages of the proposed mechanism.

Biosensors reveal where drug molecules arrive|R|74648|Researchers engineered fluorescent sensors for compounds that act at nicotinic receptors. The sensors combine a drug-binding protein with a fluorescent protein whose brightness changes after binding. They report the presence of the compound rather than the activation of a neuronal nicotinic receptor.|The original introductory movie explains this binding-dependent sensor response. Different versions could be directed to the cell surface or the endoplasmic reticulum, an internal membrane network. Their locations allowed the researchers to compare drug arrival outside the cell with access to an internal compartment.|The study examined partial agonists including dianicline and cytisine. These compounds differed in how quickly they entered the intracellular compartment. A drug can therefore bind a target in one location before reaching a similarly sensitive site behind an additional membrane barrier.

Nicotine opens nicotinic acetylcholine receptors|F|74648|Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are ion channels normally activated by acetylcholine. Nicotine can bind to them and promote channel opening, allowing positively charged ions to enter. The resulting depolarization changes activity in cells and terminals that express suitable receptor combinations.|In VTA circuits, nicotine can influence dopamine neurons directly and through their inputs. Receptors on different cell types can respond and desensitize on different timescales. The resulting dopamine output therefore reflects several cellular actions rather than one uniformly activated population.|Receptor subunits alter channel properties and drug sensitivity. Genetic variation in subunit-related genes can influence nicotine responses and risk, including pathways involving the habenula. The habenula participates in aversive regulation, adding another influence on intake beyond dopamine-related reinforcement.

The sensor changes shape when its ligand binds|R|74648|The biosensor study determined structures of its engineered drug-binding protein. A bound ligand stabilizes a different arrangement of the protein's lobes. This movement changes the environment around the attached fluorescent component and provides the basis for a measurable brightness response.|The original structural movie compares sensor conformations with and without bound ligand. It is a published molecular visualization based on the sensor structures. It does not depict a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor opening or ions moving through a neuronal membrane channel.|Separating sensor recognition from receptor activation is essential for interpreting the assay. A fluorescence increase establishes that the sensor encountered a recognized compound in that compartment. The compound's subsequent effect on a natural receptor requires a separate pharmacological or physiological measurement.

Genetic risk changes sensitivity rather than destiny|F|PLOS3003423|Genes can influence receptor composition, transmitter regulation, and the metabolism of nicotine. A variant can change the probability of developing persistent use without determining the outcome for every carrier. Access, social conditions, stress, and prior experience also influence the eventual pattern.|A receptor's subunits help determine how strongly it responds and how quickly it desensitizes. Variation affecting an aversive response can also change the balance between rewarding and unpleasant drug effects. Risk is therefore not limited to making a reward signal uniformly larger.|Gene-deletion experiments isolate particular mechanisms in a defined animal. Their results can reveal how a receptor contributes to a measured action. They do not establish that the same deletion is the ordinary cause of human tobacco use disorder or that human behavior follows an identical sequence.

Nicotine can couple normally separate motor programs|R|PLOS3003423|A study in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans examined how chronic nicotine changes coordination between behaviors. The worm normally produces rhythmic body contractions during its defecation motor program. Researchers found that nicotine increased backward movements and coupled them to these contractions.|The original wild-type recording follows repeated cycles during nicotine exposure. The visible body contraction and reversal are different actions whose timing can be compared. The experiment concerns coordination of a worm's motor programs, not a miniature model of every feature of human addiction.|The investigators identified a mechanosensory pathway from touch-receptor neurons to the AVA interneuron. Nicotine increased the pathway's responsiveness through an ACR-16 nicotinic receptor mechanism. Signals generated by the body's own contraction could consequently trigger an additional movement response.

Desensitization can occur while nicotine remains present|F|PLOS3003423|A nicotinic receptor can become less responsive during sustained agonist exposure even while nicotine remains available. This desensitized state differs from an empty receptor that has never encountered the drug. Continued exposure therefore need not produce a constant level of channel opening.|Repeated nicotine exposure can also change receptor abundance and regulation over longer periods. Increased receptor availability and acute desensitization are not contradictory because they describe different processes and timescales. The net physiological response depends on the receptor population and when it is measured.|When nicotine concentrations fall, adapted circuits operate under changed conditions and withdrawal symptoms can emerge. These symptoms can motivate further use through negative reinforcement.
